description:
Looking for a sweet, kind, patient, caring, organized, and creative teammate! 💗 Someone versatile, responsible, and fun to work with.

Skills: Strong Machine Learning & AI, Python, data analysis, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, audio processing, DSP, data sonification, sound generation, data visualization, and API integration.

Bonus: Experience with NASA datasets, music technology, or scientific data.

Curiosity, teamwork, and a positive attitude are a must!
summary: EarthSonic turns a NASA visualization listed in the Earth Information Center (EIC) gallery into an interactive listening experience. Using NASA SVS #3912, “Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature,” it samples accepted frames from the rendered video at 96 by 48 pixels. Image brightness, red–blue color balance, left–right brightness balance, and smoothed image change per source-video second update amplitude, pitch, stereo position, and modulation in a Web Audio synthesizer running in the browser. A live monitor exposes those feature-to-sound relationships as they change. Explore adds a Three.js Earth, approximate region entry points, a short listening quiz, a Science Guide, saved discoveries, personal notes, and two available one-stop expedition journeys. The project makes a scientific visualization available through both sight and sound while being explicit about the boundary between rendered pixels and ocean science: it does not load raw ECCO2 numerical fields, estimate local ocean conditions, or reproduce recorded ocean sound. Its distinctive contribution is a transparent, adjustable, real-time pixel-to-sound interpretation of a NASA global-ocean visualization.
details:
EarthSonic is a browser-based educational and artistic experience for people curious about Earth science, including students and educators. It explores how sound can offer another way to engage with a scientific visualization. This is a design goal; user impact has not been formally evaluated.

NASA source. EarthSonic uses NASA Scientific Visualization Studio item #3912, Global Sea Surface Currents and Temperature. NASA describes it as a visualization of ECCO2-modeled surface-current flows colored by corresponding sea-surface temperature. Its visualization period is March 25, 2007 through March 3, 2008. It is historical, not a live feed.

From video to sound. During playback, EarthSonic draws accepted frames from the rendered video into a 96 × 48 Canvas and calculates image features. Sampling is event-driven, with a 240 ms gate during ordinary playback—about 4.17 samples per second at most under that gate. Some media events trigger additional samples. The application does not analyze every video frame.

The analyzer calculates mean image brightness using weighted RGB luminance; average rendered RGB; the three most common of 64 coarse color bins; brightness in four screen-space quadrants; red–blue visual balance; left–right brightness balance; spatial pixel variation; a legacy frame-difference index; and a smoothed image-change rate. Only four features feed the sound mapping:

  • Brightness maps to an amplitude/gain target.
  • Red–blue channel balance maps to pitch (default range: 170–520 Hz).
  • Left–right brightness balance maps to stereo pan.
  • Smoothed mean RGB difference per elapsed video second maps to modulation rate using an artistic reference scale.

The sound uses locally synthesized Web Audio oscillators, gain and filter nodes, a stereo panner, and an analyser. Audio parameter changes are scheduled toward target values and smoothed; displayed targets are not physical measurements or instantaneous measurements of acoustic sound pressure.

What users can explore. Home introduces the method and has a muted NASA-video preview and browser spoken summary. Explore includes a Three.js globe, three approximate region entry points, Surprise Me, a one-round listening quiz, a structured Science Guide, saved regions and personal notes, and My Discoveries. Two available expeditions each have one stop; the Indian Ocean route is unavailable. Region markers are not independently calibrated to the video and do not produce local data or region-specific audio. Studio provides synchronized playback controls, four sound profiles, adjustable mapping and sound controls, a live data-to-sound monitor, and RMS, waveform, and spectrum visualizers. The persistent mini-player carries playback controls across routes. About explains the method and limitations.

The interface is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, Three.js, Lucide icons, and Tailwind CSS. It uses browser Canvas, Web Audio, Speech Synthesis, and localStorage APIs. Saved regions, personal notes, completed expeditions, and accessibility preferences are stored locally in the browser.

EarthSonic’s contribution is an adjustable, inspectable pixel-to-sound interpretation of a NASA global-ocean visualization. It does not load raw ECCO2 numerical fields, extract current velocity, or convert pixel colors into calibrated local temperatures. Image brightness and color are rendered-pixel properties; image change is not ocean-current speed; the generated sound is not a recording of the ocean. The Explore regions are approximate entry points, not local measurements. Studio’s visible muted video is a separate view of the shared analysis video; frame-perfect synchronization is not guaranteed.

The packaged local video measures VP8 WebM, 1080 × 540, 30 fps, and 66.7 seconds. NASA catalogs the matching filename at 960 × 540. Its local transformation history and byte-for-byte provenance have not been established.

Source Code: https://github.com/MEcoon/EarthSonic

AI assistance: ChatGPT and Codex assisted with research, data analysis, visual design, writing, and coding/debugging. No AI/ML model is embedded in EarthSonic, and no AI-generated images, video, or audio assets are included. The sonification is generated by EarthSonic’s Web Audio code.
